claims.text: In situ high-resolution TEM equipped with a heating stage can investigate the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at atomic resolution.
The nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt mixture stabilizes the nanoparticles' atomic structure at high temperatures.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will show minimal phase segregation up to a critical temperature.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will show minimal coarsening up to a critical temperature.
The initial nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles form a single-phase random solid solution at room temperature.
The nanoparticles will be heated in situ while their atomic lattice is continuously imaged by high-resolution TEM.
The proposed experiment uses a controlled temperature ramp from room temperature to as high as 800°C in a high-vacuum TEM environment.
Real-time TEM imaging and electron diffraction can assess atomic-lattice integrity and phase separation.
High configurational entropy in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt suppresses atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt suppresses phase segregation.
Suppressed atomic mobility and phase segregation delay nanoparticle coarsening and preserve structural homogeneity during heating.
Below a critical temperature, the nanoparticles will exhibit minimal changes in lattice spacing.
Phase separation or particle coalescence will begin only above the critical temperature.
Above the critical temperature, thermal energy may overcome entropic stabilization.
Prolonged heating may cause diffusion-controlled coarsening.
Nanoparticle size and compositional deviations may affect the observed thermal behavior.
A binary or ternary alloy prepared under similar conditions can serve as a lower-complexity control.
